nodes.question: Why are coral reefs considered important to ocean health and coastal communities?
nodes.answer: Coral reefs support a vast array of organisms, connect marine ecosystems, protect coastlines, and fuel fisheries and global tourism industries.
nodes.paragraph: Calculated expulsion rates were paired with relative symbi- ont densities in the coral tissue (symbiont/host cell ratios using quantitative PCR) and their photochemical efficiency (Fv/Fm, measured using chlorophyll fluorometry). We found that symbiont expulsion varied significantly by symbiont genus, abundance, performance, coral species, and time of day. Our findings offer insight into coral-Symbiodiniaceae homeostasis, mechanisms of coral-algal symbiosis and dys- biosis, and the potential symbiont availability and spread of symbionts in the environment and have implications for restoration approaches that involve provisioning or seeding corals with algal symbionts. Keywords Coral Symbiosis Symbiodiniaceae Expulsion Caribbean Introduction Coral reefs are integral to ocean health and the welfare of coastal communities globally, supporting a vast array of organisms, connecting tropical and sub-tropical marine ecosystems, protecting coastlines, and fueling fisheries and global tourism industries (Bruckner 2002; Brandl et al. 2019 ; Harborne et al. 2017 ; Needham 2010 ; Pascal et al. 2016). Yet, despite their immense ecological and economic importance, tropical coral reefs are in rapid decline as a result of environmental change namely global warming and anthropogenic stressors including nutrient pollution and physical destruction (Glynn 1993; Hoegh-Guldberg 1999; Hoegh-Guldberg et al.

nodes.label: Taxonomy
nodes.question: Where can Gongolaria barbata typically be found?
nodes.answer: Gongolaria barbata is usually found in very shallow, sheltered, and well-lit marine reef habitats and in coastal lagoons.
nodes.paragraph: Severe decline of Gongolaria barbata (Fucales) along most of the French Mediterranean coast Aur lie Blanfun , Charles-Fran ois Boudouresque, Marc Verlaque & Thierry Thibaut In the Mediterranean Sea, seaweed marine forests, one of the most important benthic assemblages for the coastal ecosystem functioning, are shaping the rocky reefs. Among the Fucales, Gongolaria barbata (syn. Cystoseira barbata ) is a several years living species usually growing in very shallow, sheltered and well-lit marine reef habitats and in coastal lagoons. The long-term change in its distribution in relation to a variety of disturbances has been assessed along the French Mediterranean coast, including Corsica and brackish lagoons, thanks to historical data dating back to the 19th century The current distribution was established through an extensive survey conducted by snorkelling, encompassing approximately 3 0 km of coastline. A GIS analysis indicates that Gongolaria barbata can currently be considered as regionally extinct in French Catalonia and Western Provence and functionally extinct in the French Riviera. In Languedoc, the species is extinct in the open sea and only present in certain brackish lagoons despite severe repeated anoxic crises ( mala gues ) and competition with a rich exotic flora introduced from the NE Atlantic and NW Pacific, especially the invasive Sargassum muticum.

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: In which types of habitats can Gongolaria barbata typically be found?
nodes.answer: Gongolaria barbata is typically found in very shallow, very sheltered, and well-lit reef habitats, rock-pools, and coastal lagoons.
